title: Genesis 48. The Cup of the Crossing.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 48. The Cup of the Crossing.
After these things, someone said to Joseph: Behold, your father is sick.
He took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
Someone told Jacob: Behold, your son Joseph comes to you.
And Israel strengthened himself and sat on the bed.
The old man who worshipped at the head of his bed now sits up.
He has one more thing to do.
The Cup of sojourning, held for 147 years, carried through every descent,
every deception, every reunion, has one more pour.
The father who said few and evil have been my days now gathers the strength to bless the next generation.
Jacob said to Joseph:
El Shaddai appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me.
And said to me: Behold, I will make you fruitful,
and multiply you,
and I will make of you a company of peoples,
and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.
El Shaddai.
Luz.
Bethel.
The dream.
The ladder.
The angels ascending and descending.
The promise.
Jacob is passing the Bethel promise to the next generation.
The covenant given to him as a fugitive with a stone for a pillow is now being transferred to his grandsons on his deathbed.
The Cup that was poured at Bethel, the if, the vow,
the stone, the oil, now reaches its destination.
The promise does not die with the patriarch.
It crosses.
Your two sons,
who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you into Egypt,
are mine.
Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, will be mine.
Jacob adopts Joseph's sons.
They become tribes.
Not sons of Joseph, sons of Jacob.
The twelve tribes will include Ephraim and Manasseh.
Joseph gets a double portion through his sons.
The firstborn's inheritance, though Judah carries the covenant line.
The Cup that was held by twelve sons now expands to include two grandsons born in Egypt.
The covenant does not stay in the bloodline of Canaan.
It adopts.
Ephraim and Manasseh are half-Egyptian, their mother is Asenath,
daughter of an Egyptian priest.
The covenant adopts the foreign-born into the promise.
As for me, when I came from Paddan,
Rachel died beside me in the land of Canaan, on the way,
when there was still some distance to come to Ephrath.
And I buried her there on the way to Ephrath, that is,
Bethlehem.
Rachel's death.
The wound that never closed.
Jacob buried her on the road, not in the family tomb,
not at Machpelah.
She died giving birth to Benjamin.
Now Jacob is blessing Rachel's firstborn's sons, grandchildren she never met.
The mother who said God has taken away my reproach and named him Joseph,
may the Lord add.
The Lord added.
Two more.
Rachel's line grows through the grandsons she never held.
The Cup that was emptied on the road to Bethlehem is now refilled in Egypt with two boys who carry Rachel's fruitfulness across generations.
Israel saw Joseph's sons and said: Who are these?
Joseph said to his father: They are my sons,
whom God has given me here.
He said: Please bring them to me, and I will bless them.
Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age,
so that he could not see well.
His eyes are dim.
Like Isaac.
The father who could not see and was deceived by Jacob.
The same blindness.
The same age.
The same deathbed blessing of a younger over an older.
But Jacob is not Isaac.
Isaac was blind and deceived.
Jacob is blind and prophetic.
Joseph brought them near to him.
He kissed them and embraced them.
Israel said to Joseph: I didn't think I would see your face,
and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.
The Cup of reunion overflows into the third generation.
The father who thought his son was dead now sees his son's sons.
The eyes that wept over a blood-stained coat now behold the faces of grandchildren.
The blindness that could have been Isaac's curse becomes Jacob's gift,
he does not see with his eyes.
He sees with prophecy.
Joseph brought them out from between his knees,
and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
Joseph took them both,
Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand,
and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand,
and brought them near to him.
The older on the right.
The younger on the left.
The proper arrangement.
Manasseh, the firstborn, at the right hand, where the greater blessing belongs.
Ephraim, the younger, at the left.
Joseph arranges them correctly.
The way it should be.
But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on Ephraim's head,
who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh's head.
He guided his hands knowingly, Manasseh was the firstborn.
for He crossed his hands.
Deliberately.
he made his hands cross.
With knowledge.
With intention.
The crossing.
In chapter twenty-seven, Jacob deceived blind Isaac with goatskins on his hands.
The hands that felt like Esau's.
The hands that carried a lie.
Now Jacob, also blind, crosses his hands deliberately.
The same gesture.
The same action.
The same blind father.
The same younger-over older.
But the direction has changed.
The crossing that was deception, Jacob pretending to be Esau,
is now prophecy, Jacob deliberately choosing the younger over the older.
The deceiver becomes the prophet.
The same hands.
The same crossing.
Turned toward truth.
The younger over the older.
One last time.
Isaac over Ishmael.
Jacob over Esau.
Joseph over his older brothers.
Now Ephraim over Manasseh.
The pattern that has defined the covenant's path since Abraham,
God choosing the younger, reaches its final expression.
And this time it is done openly, deliberately, without deception.
Jacob, who stole the blessing through trickery, now gives it through prophecy.
The Cup of the crossing is the deceiver's redemption, the same hands,
the same gesture, but turned toward truth.
When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim,
it displeased him.
He held up his father's hand to remove it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head.
Joseph said to his father: Not so, my father,
for this is the firstborn.
Put your right hand on his head.
Joseph tries to correct.
The same instinct that made him arrange the boys properly,
older on the right, younger on the left.
Joseph wants the right thing done the right way.
But the right thing is not always the prophetic thing.
His father refused and said: I know, my son, I know.
He also will become a people, and he also will be great.
However, his younger brother will be greater than he,
and his offspring will become a multitude of nations.
I know.
I know, my son, I know.
Isaac said: Are you really my son Esau?
He did not know.
Jacob says: I know.
The blind patriarch sees more clearly than any seeing man.
The deception that required blindness in chapter twenty-seven is replaced by prophecy that works through blindness in chapter forty-eight.
The same blindness.
Different authority.
The man who used blindness to deceive now uses blindness to prophesy.
He blessed them that day, saying: Israel will bless in you, saying,
God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.
He set Ephraim before Manasseh.
Ephraim before Manasseh.
The younger first.
The pattern sealed in the blessing formula for all generations.
Every time Israel blesses a child, they will say:
May God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.
The younger's name comes first.
Forever.
The crossing of hands becomes the crossing of generations,
the younger-before-older embedded in the blessing itself.
Then Jacob spoke his last blessing, the most personal prayer in Genesis:
The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked,
the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,
the Angel who redeems me from all evil,
may He bless the boys.
May my name be named on them,
and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac.
Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.
Three titles for God.
Three layers of the Cup.
The God who has been my shepherd.
the shepherd.
The man whose sons are shepherds, who lives among shepherds,
whose family is an abomination to Egyptians because they are shepherds,
calls God his shepherd.
The man who said few and evil have been my days now says God shepherded him through all of it.
The Cup that held hardship for 147 years is now acknowledged as held by a shepherd who never left.
The Angel who redeems me from all evil.
the go'el.
The kinsman-redeemer.
First use of go'el in Genesis.
Jacob acknowledges: evil happened.
And God redeemed him from it.
Not prevented it, redeemed him from it.
The Cup of evil was real.
The redemption was real.
Both true, like Joseph's: they sold me, AND God sent me.
Jacob does not say: God protected me from all evil.
He says: God redeemed me from all evil.
The evil happened.
The redemption happened.
The Cup holds both.
May my name be named on them.
The covenant name, Israel, placed on Joseph's Egyptian born sons.
The covenant does not stay in the bloodline of Canaan.
It adopts.
The foreign-born are grafted in.
The Cup that crossed from Canaan to Egypt now crosses from Hebrew to half-Egyptian.
The promise is not bound by blood or geography.
It is bound by God.
Israel said to Joseph: Behold, I am dying.
But God will be with you,
and bring you again to the land of your fathers.
The same promise God gave Jacob in chapter forty-six:
I will go down with you, and I will bring you up.
Now Jacob passes it to Joseph: God will bring you back.
The Cup of sojourning, held in Egypt, pointing to Canaan,
is passed to the next generation.
The father dies.
The promise lives.
The bones will travel.
Moreover I have given to you one portion more than your brothers,
Shechem,
which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.
Shechem.
The place where Dinah was violated.
Where Simeon and Levi slaughtered a city,
where Jacob buried the foreign gods under the oak,
where he built an altar and named it El Elohe Yisrael.
Now Jacob gives it to Joseph as an extra portion.
The place of violence becomes the place of inheritance.
The land stained by the brothers' blood becomes the land given to the brother who was betrayed.
The Cup that was stained at Shechem is now planted at Shechem,
as a promise, as a portion,
as the first fruits of the land that will be returned to.
The Cup of the crossing.
The deceiver's hands,
the hands that wore goatskins to fool a blind father,
now cross deliberately to bless.
The same gesture.
Different direction.
The hands that took a blessing by fraud now give a blessing by prophecy.
The blindness that hid truth now reveals it.
The crossing that was deception's tool becomes redemption's signature.
Jacob's whole life is in this gesture.
The heel-catcher who reached for his brother's heel in the womb.
The grabber who took a birthright and a blessing.
The wrestler who held on to God and would not let go.
The hands that deceived Isaac now cross to prophesy over Ephraim and Manasseh.
The hands that held the Cup through every chapter,
from the stone at Bethel to the bed in Egypt,
now pour the blessing on the next generation.
The God who shepherded me.
The Angel who redeemed me.
The Cup holds.
The crossing is complete.
The deceiver has become the prophet.
The same hands.
Turned toward truth.
